```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

```

```{r setup}
library(codeminer)

create_dummy_database()
```

Every query function has sensible defaults: the latest version of each table,
and the column filters the table author registered (active SNOMED CT
relationships, assured mappings, and so on). This guide is about changing those
defaults when a piece of work needs something else, and about doing it once
rather than on every call. `vignette("col_filters")` is the reference for how
filters are modelled; this vignette works through the common tasks.

# Three places to set things

Each setting can be made at three levels. The narrowest one that names a
table wins:

| Level | Versions | Column filters |
|---|---|---|
| One call | `lookup_version = `, `relationship_version = `, `map_version = ` | `col_filters = ` |
| The session | `codeminer_set_version()` | `codeminer_set_col_filters()`, `with_col_filters()` |
| A script | `options(codeminer.lookup_version = ...)` etc. | `options(codeminer.col_filters = ...)` |

So the order of precedence for filters is: the `col_filters` argument (or an
enclosing `with_col_filters()`), then session pins, then the
`codeminer.col_filters` option, then the defaults registered in the database.
For versions it is the argument, then `codeminer_set_version()` pins, then the
`codeminer.*_version` options, then `"latest"`.

The options a script can set, all read when a query runs:

| Option | Default | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `codeminer.code_type` | unset | `type` on lookup and relationship queries (not `MAP()`) |
| `codeminer.map_from`, `codeminer.map_to` | unset | `from` and `to` in `MAP()` |
| `codeminer.lookup_version` | `"latest"` | `lookup_version` |
| `codeminer.relationship_version` | `"latest"` | `relationship_version` |
| `codeminer.map_version` | `"latest"` | `map_version` in `MAP()` |
| `codeminer.col_filters` | unset | `col_filters`, when a call leaves it at `"default"` |
| `codeminer.max_traversal_nodes` | `20000` | `max_nodes` on hierarchy queries |
| `codeminer.max_tree_codes` | `10000` | `max_codes` in `get_relationship_tree()` |
| `codeminer.chunk_batch_size`, `codeminer.max_leaf_rows`, `codeminer.max_chunk_matches` | `200000`, `30000`, `20000` | the `*_CHUNK` paging functions |

Put the options at the top of a script, in the same block that attaches the
package, so anyone reading the script sees what every result depends on.
`codeminer_status()` prints the pins and the filter option in force.

# Use a specific table version

A database can hold several versions of a lookup, relationship or mapping
table. `"latest"` is resolved once per session and cached, so a script is
consistent, but a result you want to reproduce later should name its version.

```{r versions}
# What is in the database, and which version "latest" currently means
get_codeminer_metadata("lookup")[, c("code_type", "lookup_version")]

# Pin one code type for the session
codeminer_set_version(lookup = c("ICD-10" = "UKB v4"))
codeminer_status()

codeminer_clear_versions()
```

The `codeminer.lookup_version`, `codeminer.relationship_version` and
`codeminer.map_version` options set one version string for every code type,
which suits a database built from a single release:

```r
options(codeminer.lookup_version = "UKB v4", codeminer.map_version = "UKB v4")
```

Pins are per code type, so when different code types need different versions,
use `codeminer_set_version()` in the setup block instead. An explicit
`lookup_version = ` argument always wins over both.

# The SNOMED CT filters

The remaining scenarios are about SNOMED CT, whose tables carry `active` flags
that are filtered by default. The dummy database used in this vignette has no
SNOMED CT, so the evaluated examples register a tiny table shaped like it, and
each one is followed by the command to run against a real database. Discover a
real database's filters with:

```r
get_col_filters(defaults_only = FALSE)
```

On a database built from the UK SNOMED CT release that returns, among others:

| Table | Column | Values | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lookup` / `"SNOMED CT"` | `active_concept` | `0`, `1` | both |
| `lookup` / `"SNOMED CT"` | `active_description` | `0`, `1` | `1` |
| `lookup` / `"SNOMED CT"` | `moduleId_concept` | the release's module ids | all of them |
| `relationship` / `"SNOMED CT"` | `active` | `0`, `1` | `1` |
| `mapping` / `"SNOMED CT > ICD-10"` and others | `active` | `0`, `1` | `1` |

```{r demo-lookup}
# A lookup shaped like the SNOMED CT one: concepts and descriptions carry
# active flags, and each concept belongs to a module.
demo <- data.frame(
  code = c("100", "100", "200", "300", "D1", "D2", "DF1"),
  description = c(
    "Warfarin", "Warfarin (old term)", "Heparin", "Aspirin",
    "Anticoagulant", "Antiplatelet", "Oral tablet"
  ),
  active_concept = c("1", "1", "0", "1", "1", "1", "1"),
  active_description = c("1", "0", "1", "1", "1", "1", "1"),
  module = c("core", "core", "core", "drug", "core", "core", "core")
)
add_lookup_table(
  demo,
  lookup_metadata(
    "Demo SCT",
    col_filters = list(
      active_concept = list(
        values = c("0", "1"),
        defaults = c("0", "1"),
        description = "Whether the concept is active in the release."
      ),
      active_description = list(
        values = c("0", "1"),
        defaults = "1",
        description = "Whether the description (term) is active."
      ),
      module = list(
        values = c("core", "drug"),
        defaults = c("core", "drug"),
        description = "Module the concept belongs to."
      )
    )
  )
)
```

## Include inactive descriptions, or restrict to one module

By default each concept returns with its active descriptions only. To see
retired terms as well, un-filter `active_description`; to work with the UK
drug extension only, narrow the module column. Both are table-keyed entries
under `lookup`:

```{r lookup-filters}
# Default: active descriptions
CODES("all", type = "Demo SCT", preferred_description_only = FALSE)

# Retired terms too, for this call
CODES(
  "all",
  type = "Demo SCT",
  preferred_description_only = FALSE,
  col_filters = list(lookup = list("Demo SCT" = list(active_description = NA)))
)

# One module only, for the whole script
options(
  codeminer.col_filters = list(lookup = list("Demo SCT" = list(module = "drug")))
)
CODES("all", type = "Demo SCT")

options(codeminer.col_filters = NULL)
```

Note what the second call did: an entry for a table *replaces* that table's
default filters wholesale, so naming only `active_description = NA` also
dropped the default `module` filter. That is harmless here, because the module
default includes every value, but when a table has several restrictive defaults
start from `get_col_filters()` and amend it (see `vignette("col_filters")`,
"Amending filters").

On a real database:

```r
# Retired descriptions too
options(codeminer.col_filters = list(
  lookup = list("SNOMED CT" = list(active_description = NA))
))

# UK drug extension only
options(codeminer.col_filters = list(
  lookup = list("SNOMED CT" = list(moduleId_concept = "999000011000001104"))
))
```

## Include inactive relationships

Relationships carry an `active` flag and queries use active ones by default.
That is right for a current hierarchy, but it hides retired links: a product
withdrawn years ago still appears in old records, and its "has active
ingredient" relationship is inactive, so a prescription list built from
ingredients misses it. Un-filter the relationship table, and only that table,
for the whole script:

```{r demo-relationship}
rel <- data.frame(
  from = c("100", "200", "300", "100"),
  to = c("D1", "D1", "D2", "DF1"),
  type = c("is a", "is a", "is a", "has dose form"),
  active = c("1", "0", "1", "1")
)
add_relationship_table(
  rel,
  relationship_metadata(
    "Demo SCT",
    type_col = "type",
    child_parent_relationship_code = "is a",
    col_filters = list(
      active = list(
        values = c("0", "1"),
        defaults = "1",
        description = "Whether the relationship edge is active.",
        value_labels = c("1" = "Active", "0" = "Inactive")
      )
    )
  )
)

# Default: only the active "is a" link reaches Warfarin
CHILDREN("D1", type = "Demo SCT")

# The script-wide setting: all relationships, lookup filters untouched
options(
  codeminer.col_filters = list(relationship = list("Demo SCT" = NA))
)
CHILDREN("D1", type = "Demo SCT")
```

Keep `codeminer.col_filters` set for the rest of the recipe, so every
`CHILDREN()`, `PARENTS()`, `ATTRIBUTES_FOR()` and `HAS_ATTRIBUTES()` call sees
the same relationships. Don't reach for `col_filters = NA` instead: that turns
off the *lookup* filters too, which returns retired descriptions as extra rows
and changes the row count of every result.

On a real database:

```r
options(codeminer.col_filters = list(relationship = list("SNOMED CT" = NA)))
```

## Restrict relationship types

Relationship *types* are not a filter. They are the `relationship_types`
argument of `ATTRIBUTES_FOR()` and `HAS_ATTRIBUTES()`, because which types
matter differs from one question to the next within the same recipe
(ingredients for one part, dose forms for another). `RELATIONSHIP_TYPES_TO()`
lists the types that point at a code:

```{r relationship-types}
RELATIONSHIP_TYPES_TO("DF1", type = "Demo SCT")

ATTRIBUTES_FOR("100", type = "Demo SCT", relationship_types = "has dose form")
```

The `codeminer.col_filters` option set above is still in force, so these
calls also use inactive relationships. Clear it when a recipe moves on:

```{r clear-option}
options(codeminer.col_filters = NULL)
```

## Include inactive map rows

Mapping tables have filters of their own. The dummy database's Read v3 to
ICD-10 map registers `mapping_status`, selecting exact, general and default
mappings; SNOMED CT maps register `active`, selecting active rows. The key is
the `"from > to"` pair:

```{r mapping-filters}
nrow(MAP("all", from = "Read v3", to = "ICD-10"))

# Every row, whatever its status, for the rest of the script
options(
  codeminer.col_filters = list(mapping = list("Read v3 > ICD-10" = NA))
)
nrow(MAP("all", from = "Read v3", to = "ICD-10"))

options(codeminer.col_filters = NULL)
```

On a real database:

```r
options(codeminer.col_filters = list(mapping = list("SNOMED CT > ICD-10" = NA)))
```

# Settings and the rest of the session

The option is the lowest-priority setting, so anything you do in the session
still works as before while it is set:

- A `col_filters` argument on one call, or a `with_col_filters()` block,
  overrides it for the tables it names.
- A `codeminer_set_col_filters()` pin overrides it for the tables it names.
  `codeminer_set_col_filters(NA)` turns all filtering off and leaves the
  option unread until `codeminer_clear_col_filters()`.
- Tables the option does not name keep their registered defaults.

Two things to know:

- `options(codeminer.col_filters = NULL)` *removes* the option, which returns
  to the defaults. To turn all filtering off through the option, use
  `options(codeminer.col_filters = NA)`.
- The value is checked at the first query that uses it. A misspelt code type
  is a warning, and the query runs with the defaults for that table; a
  misspelt top-level name (anything other than `lookup`, `relationship` and
  `mapping`) is an error. A misspelt option *name* is silent, as with any R
  option, so copy the name from here.

# Storing settings in a recipe

A recipe's setup block is the place for every setting that changes results:

```r
library(codeminer)
options(
  codeminer.code_type = "SNOMED CT",
  codeminer.col_filters = list(relationship = list("SNOMED CT" = NA))
)
codeminer_set_version(
  lookup = c("SNOMED CT" = "uk_sct2mo_43.1.0_20261021000001Z.zip"),
  relationship = c("SNOMED CT" = "uk_sct2mo_43.1.0_20261021000001Z.zip")
)
```

For a project that shares settings between scripts, keep them in a JSON file
and read it in the setup block. Filter objects round-trip through
`jsonlite::toJSON()` and `jsonlite::fromJSON()` (see `vignette("col_filters")`,
"The round-trip guarantee"), and `vignette("codeminer")` shows the same
pattern for version pins.

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
options(codeminer.col_filters = NULL)
codeminer_clear_col_filters()
codeminer_clear_versions()
```
